subject: Mathematics
topic: Quadratic forms, roots, turning points and discriminants
scope: Original partial support for AQA 8300 A11/A18, Cambridge 0580 Extended E2.5.6 (2025-2027), and the digital SAT nonlinear equation/function skills. Higher-level algebra is labelled in the crosswalk; this is not a whole-course or official scoring claim.
prerequisites: Expand two binomials and factor a common factor.
Work with square roots and solve simple linear equations.
objectives: Derive roots using factorisation, square completion or the formula.
Connect a discriminant and a turning point to a graph.
Check domain constraints in a quadratic model.

notes.heading: Three forms answer different questions
paragraphs: A quadratic function has the form f(x)=ax²+bx+c with a≠0. In expanded form, c is the vertical intercept and a controls opening direction and vertical scaling. In factored form a(x-r)(x-s), the real zeros r and s are visible. In vertex form a(x-h)²+k, the turning point is (h,k). These are different representations of one relationship, not different functions. A quadratic without real roots cannot be factored into real linear factors, but it still has a real vertex.

Choose a representation based on the question rather than converting mechanically. To locate zeros, a correct factorisation may be quickest. To find a minimum or maximum, completed-square form reveals the answer without numerical guessing. To evaluate at x=0, expanded form is convenient. Always preserve the leading coefficient during a conversion. Writing x²-6x+11 as (x-3)²+11 is incorrect because expansion introduces an extra 9.

notes.heading: Factorisation and the zero-product condition
paragraphs: The zero-product principle says that if a product of real numbers is zero, at least one factor is zero. It applies after the equation is rearranged so one side is zero. From (x-2)(x+5)=6 you cannot infer x=2 or x=-5. First expand or otherwise rearrange the full equation. For x²+3x-10=0, the factorisation (x+5)(x-2)=0 does yield the two roots. Substitute each root into the original equation to check the algebra.

When a leading coefficient is not 1, a pair of factors must reproduce both the middle term and the constant. It is not enough for the constants to multiply correctly. If no simple integer factorisation is apparent, use another method instead of forcing approximate factors. Repeated factors such as (x-4)² give a repeated root, not two distinct x-intercepts.

notes.heading: Completing the square with a coefficient
paragraphs: For x²+px+q, add and subtract (p/2)² to obtain (x+p/2)²+q-(p/2)². This preserves the original expression because the added and subtracted quantities cancel. If the coefficient of x² is not 1, factor it from the x² and x terms first. For 2x²-12x+7, write 2(x²-6x)+7=2[(x-3)²-9]+7=2(x-3)²-11. The turning point is (3,-11), and because 2 is positive this is a minimum.

Solving a completed-square equation requires both square-root signs. From (x-h)²=m with m>0, x=h±√m. If m=0 there is one repeated root; if m<0 there are no real solutions. Do not confuse the sign inside the bracket with the vertex coordinate: x+3 means h=-3. The square is nonnegative, which is why a positive leading coefficient places the vertex below or at every other point.

notes.heading: Formula and discriminant
paragraphs: The quadratic formula gives x=(-b±√(b²-4ac))/(2a) for ax²+bx+c=0 with a≠0. Put the entire numerator over 2a. Parentheses matter when b is negative: -b becomes positive, while b² is nonnegative. The discriminant D=b²-4ac determines the number of distinct real roots: two if D>0, one repeated root if D=0, and none if D<0. This counts real roots; it does not say the function itself is undefined when D<0.

A positive perfect-square discriminant guarantees rational roots when the coefficients are rational, but not necessarily integer roots. Whether a root is an integer also depends on the denominator. A non-square positive discriminant with integer coefficients generally leaves a surd expression. Retaining that expression can be more precise than rounding early. When decimals are requested, round at the end and use substitution or the graph's symmetry as a check.

notes.heading: Models, restrictions and reasonableness
paragraphs: A quadratic model may describe an area, height or other quantity only on a restricted domain. Algebra can return roots outside that physical domain. Explain why a root is rejected using the context, such as a negative length, rather than deleting it without comment. The vertex may also lie outside the permitted interval; in that case it need not be the model's maximum or minimum over the allowed values. Compare the endpoints as well when a closed interval is given.

The axis of symmetry x=-b/(2a) gives another consistency check. If there are two real roots, their midpoint lies on this axis. A graph should open in the direction implied by a and cross the vertical axis at c. These independent features can reveal a transcription error even before a final calculation. A context description still needs to justify why a quadratic model is appropriate; a neat parabola is not evidence that real observations follow it exactly.

notes.heading: Scope and deliberate practice
paragraphs: AQA separates elementary factorisation from its Higher-tier completion-of-square and formula work. Cambridge E2.5.6 here refers to the Extended 2025-2027 syllabus; the mapping includes only quadratic solving and completed-square structure, not every equation requirement. The SAT references cover selected nonlinear equation and function skills and do not imply a complete digital test simulation.

For revision, take one expression and identify what each form makes visible. Then solve a different quadratic using two methods and check that the resulting root sets agree. Explain the discriminant before calculating decimal roots. Keep written reasoning for contextual exclusions, because a numeric match alone cannot show that a root was interpreted correctly.

notes.heading: Reading a repeated root from equivalent forms
paragraphs: A quadratic with a repeated real root touches the horizontal axis at its turning point rather than crossing it. Factored form, completed-square form and the discriminant describe the same situation in different ways. Match coefficients carefully when comparing a perfect square with the original expression, especially when the leading coefficient is not one. A zero discriminant gives one distinct real root with multiplicity two; it does not give two different roots or no roots. Expanding a proposed factorisation is a useful independent check. The sign of the leading coefficient then identifies whether the touching point is a minimum or maximum.

workedExamples.prompt: Write x²+8x+5 in vertex form and state its minimum.
steps: The square is smallest at x=-4.
Check x=-1/3 and x=2 in the original equation.

workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular area is A=x(14-x) for 0≤x≤14. Find the maximum.
steps: The permitted value x=7 makes the square zero.
workedExamples.answer: Maximum area 49 square units, with x=7.

workedExamples.prompt: For f(x) = 4x² - 12x + 9, write a squared form, find its root and turning point, and state whether the graph crosses the x-axis.
workedExamples.answer: f(x) = (2x - 3)². The repeated root is x = 3/2; the turning point is (3/2, 0), and the graph touches without crossing.
steps: The square is nonnegative and zero only there, so the point is a minimum and there is no sign change.

misconceptions.claim: A factored expression always lets you set its factors to zero.
A positive discriminant means two integer roots.
misconceptions.correction: It means two distinct real roots; integrality requires additional conditions.

misconceptions.claim: Every algebraic root is physically valid.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the model's units and domain restrictions.

flashcards.front: What decides whether a parabola's vertex is a minimum or maximum?

flashcards.front: Why keep a surd root during working?
flashcards.back: It preserves exactness until rounding is required.

questions.prompt: What is the vertex of f(x)=2(x+3)²-5?
solution: The square is zero at x=-3.
At that x, f(x)=-5.

questions.prompt: Find the minimum value of x²-10x+13.
solution: Write x²-10x+13=(x-5)²-12.
The square has minimum zero at x=5.
Factor as (2x-3)(x+2)=0.
Set each factor equal to zero.
markingPoints: Factor or apply another valid exact method.

questions.prompt: For x²-6x+k=0 to have a repeated root, find k.
solution: Set the discriminant 36-4k equal to zero.
Solve k=9 and check (x-3)²=0.

questions.prompt: A learner says x²+4x+8 has no graph because its discriminant is negative. Correct the reasoning.
questions.answer: It has a real graph y=(x+2)²+4 with minimum 4. A negative discriminant says the equation y=0 has no real roots, not that the function has no real values.
solution: Separate a function from its zero equation.
Complete the square.
Explain the absence of horizontal-axis intersections.
Rewrite as (x-2)²=5.
Take both square roots and isolate x.
markingPoints: Complete the square or use the formula.

questions.prompt: A rectangle has sides x and 18-x, with 2≤x≤6. Does the unrestricted vertex give its allowed maximum area?
questions.answer: No. The unrestricted vertex is x=9, outside the domain. On [2,6] the area increases, so the maximum is 6×12=72.
solution: Write A=81-(x-9)².
Locate the vertex outside the permitted interval.
On this interval the squared distance to 9 is least at x=6.

questions.prompt: Explain why x=2 and x=-3 do not solve (x-2)(x+3)=4.
questions.answer: Each makes the left side zero, not 4. Rearrange to x²+x-10=0 before solving.
solution: Substitute either claimed root.
State the missing zero-product condition.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = 4x² - 12x + 9, write a squared form, find its root and turning point, and state whether the graph crosses the x-axis.
questions.answer: f(x) = (2x - 3)². The repeated root is x = 3/2; the turning point is (3/2, 0), and the graph touches without crossing.
solution: Recognise 4x² - 12x + 9 as (2x - 3)².
Set 2x - 3 = 0 to obtain x = 3/2.
The square is nonnegative and zero only there, so the point is a minimum and there is no sign change.
markingPoints: The square is nonnegative and zero only there, so the point is a minimum and there is no sign change.

questions.prompt: A learner calculates discriminant zero and concludes there are no real solutions. Correct the rule and verify it for 4x² - 12x + 9 = 0.
questions.answer: Zero discriminant means one repeated real root; the quadratic formula gives x = 12/8 = 3/2.
solution: The discriminant is (-12)² - 4 × 4 × 9 = 0.
The plus and minus branches of the formula coincide when the square root is zero.
Both give 12/(2 × 4) = 3/2, not an absence of real solutions.
markingPoints: The plus and minus branches of the formula coincide when the square root is zero.
Both give 12/(2 × 4) = 3/2, not an absence of real solutions.
